notes: The breakout's 6-pin header is plugged into breadboard row j, columns 4-9 (ST, Z, Y, X, GND, VDD). The image's upper half (rows f-j) is bank 'b' in the catalogue naming. Each jumper wire goes into the same column in a different row of the same strip. The exact rows are read from the picture and are approximate.

A4 is driven LOW as ground and A5 HIGH as 5 V (digital pins 18 and 19). Both connections are made with jumper wires to the Uno's analog pins, as in the tutorial. Z, Y and X go to A1, A2 and A3, following the circuit image and the pin table. The schematic's X/Z crossing is not followed.
The tutorial warns that some ADXL3xx breakouts need a 3.3 V supply and can be damaged by 5 V. The SparkFun breakout shown runs from the 5 V on A5, as the tutorial describes.
The tutorial lists no resistors, LEDs or buttons, so none are added.

Breadboard placement read from the circuit image: resistor spans columns 3 and 6 in the top half; LED legs in columns 6 (anode, bent leg, joined to resistor) and 8 (cathode, to GND); the pot straddles the centre gap with its wiper in column 23 (top half) and its outer pins in columns 22 and 24 (bottom half).
Row letters within each column-bank are arbitrary choices since all 5 holes in a column-bank are one strip; the image labels rows differently from the catalogue naming.
The 220 ohm resistor feeds the LED anode from pin 9; the LED cathode goes to GND, as in the text and schematic.
The black wire on the digital header uses GND.3 (next to AREF/pin 13); the power header GND is GND.1.
The pot's outer pins are interchangeable; GND went to column 22 and VCC (5V) to column 24 per the image.

The tutorial offers two alternatives (potentiometer, or photoresistor + 10k resistor). The main circuit text describes the potentiometer, so that circuit is built; the photoresistor variant is not included.

Breadboard coordinates follow the potentiometer image, which is drawn rotated relative to the catalogue naming: the pot's two outer pins are in the image's lower half (rows a-e, bank 't', columns 10 and 12) and its wiper is in the upper half (bank 'b', column 11). Black wire (GND) is on column 10 and red wire (5V) on column 12, as drawn.

The built-in LED on pin 13 is not modelled as a separate part. The optional external circuit (220 ohm resistor and red LED) is included: pin 13 -> resistor -> LED anode, LED cathode -> GND. It has no image, so its breadboard positions and the use of GND.2 (the GND next to pin 13) are assumed.
The pot's GND/VCC ports are symmetric, so the end-for-end assignment of the outer pins is interchangeable.

Potentiometer legs are placed in columns 10, 11, 12 of the bottom half of the breadboard (row f), with jumper wires in row j of the same columns; exact columns/rows are read from the image and approximate.
Outer pin to GND, other outer pin to 5V, wiper (middle pin) to A0, as the manual states. The pot's GND and VCC are symmetric so which outer pin goes to which supply is interchangeable.
Hardware list has only the Arduino board and the potentiometer; the breadboard and three jumper wires are shown in the circuit image.

The tutorial shows several programmer/target pairings (Uno-Uno, Uno-Nano, Mega-Uno, MKR1000-Uno). I built one: an Arduino Uno as the ISP programmer and an Arduino Nano as the target. The Tools menu screenshot selects Board: Arduino Nano, Processor: ATmega328P, Programmer: Arduino as ISP.

I used the 'old style' wiring from the text: D13 to D13 (SCK), D12 to D12 (MISO), D11 to D11 (MOSI), D10 on the programmer to RESET on the target, plus 5V to 5V and GND to GND. This is equivalent to the ICSP wiring.

The 10 µF electrolytic capacitor is included because the text says boards with a USB interface chip (Uno, Nano, Mega, Mini) need it on the programmer. Positive leg goes to the programmer's RESET and negative to its GND. It is fitted after the ArduinoISP sketch is uploaded. I plugged its legs straight into the Uno header sockets.

The text says the sketch supports three optional status LEDs but gives no pins or values. I used the ArduinoISP sketch defaults: heartbeat on D9, error on D8, programming on D7. I added a 220 Ω series resistor to ground for each LED, and put them on a breadboard to match the 'Arduino_ISP_LEDSOK' picture. The resistor value and breadboard layout are my assumptions.
The tutorial's images (memory map, Tools menu) are not wiring diagrams, so they add no connections. The ICSP header variant and the Mega, MKR1000 and Uno-to-Uno variants are not built.
The tutorial says not to power the boards while wiring, so no USB cable is modelled.
All part types (arduino-mega, led, resistor, breadboard, jumper-wire) exist in the catalogue, so no lookup was needed.
The expanded part and edge lists are used instead of a repeat. Each LED unit sits in different breadboard columns, and a repeat would need an attach override for every breadboard port in every copy.

The exact breadboard holes are my own tidy layout, not a copy of the picture. LED k uses columns 2k-1 (anode strip) and 2k (cathode strip). Each 220 ohm resistor spans the centre gap in the anode column. Pin wires land in the lower bank of the same column.
LED k is driven by Mega pin k+1, so pins 2 to 13 each drive one LED through its own 220 ohm resistor.

Each cathode column is wired to the top negative rail (tn.<column>) with a black jumper. One black jumper takes GND.1 of the Mega to the same rail. The picture shows the GND pin next to AREF, and the catalogue name GND.1 is my assumption for it.
The hook-up wires are all modelled as jumper-wire. Every inserted lead or wire end gets both a joined and an electrical edge.

The tutorial has two wiring diagrams (burn bootloader; upload via USB-serial). I built the first: the bootloader-burning (ArduinoISP) circuit with the external 16 MHz clock. The upload circuit (RX/TX wires, Arduino microcontroller removed) and the minimal no-crystal circuit are not included.
The 10k pull-up resistor from ATmega pin 1 (RESET) to +5V is drawn in the image and listed in the parts list.
Arduino pin 10 goes to ATmega pin 1 (RESET), pin 11 to pin 17 (MOSI), pin 12 to pin 18 (MISO), pin 13 to pin 19 (SCK), as in the standard ArduinoISP wiring.
The crystal sits across ATmega pins 9 and 10 (XTAL1/XTAL2) via the two blue wires; each 22 pF capacitor goes from a crystal leg to ground.
Exact breadboard hole positions and rail indices are estimated from the picture. The chip straddles the centre gap, with pins 1-14 on the bottom half and 15-28 on the top half.

The image shows no clear AVCC (pin 20) or second GND (pin 22 is grounded, pin 8 also) wire beyond what is drawn. I added only the visible power wires: +5V to pin 7 and GND to pins 8 and 22. A real build should also connect pin 20 (AVCC) to +5V.
Top rail 'tp' is +5V and 'tn' is GND, linked to the bottom rails 'bp' and 'bn' by the long red and black wires on the right.
The Blink example uses the on-board LED; the optional external LED circuit (LED + 220 ohm resistor) is what is built here.

Breadboard coordinates are read from the image: the upper half is labelled rows f-j, so it is mapped to bank 'b' (rows f-j). The strip for column 3 joins the orange wire (3b.g) and resistor leg 1 (3b.h). The strip for column 8 joins the LED cathode (8b.i) and the black wire (8b.g).
The LED's bent (long) leg in column 6 is taken as the anode, in line with the text. The resistor links pin 13 to the anode. The cathode returns to the GND pin next to pin 13 (GND.1).
The Uno is not powered by a USB cable in the figures, so none is added.
All parts exist in the catalogue, so no lookup was needed.

The catalogue names the breadboard's top half bank 't' (rows a-e) and its bottom half bank 'b' (rows f-j). The picture labels the rows the other way round (j-f on top, e-a on bottom). I used the catalogue naming. The top half holds the LEDs, the black wires and the resistors' upper legs. The bottom half holds the resistors' lower legs and the blue wires.

From the circuit image, each LED's anode (the longer leg, which bends toward the resistor) is in the same column as its resistor's top leg. The cathode is in the next column. A black jumper runs from each cathode column to the top ground rail (tn). Arduino GND goes to the same rail, as in the schematic.
Pin-to-LED mapping follows the image and schematic: pin 7 goes to the first LED (breadboard column 7), then pins 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 to columns 10, 13, 16, 19 and 22.
The image shows 220 ohm resistors, as the schematic says. The anode/cathode assignment follows the schematic symbol direction (pin, resistor, anode, cathode, GND).
Rail hole numbers (tn.8, tn.11 and so on) are approximate. Each rail is one strip, so the exact hole does not change the circuit.
The Arduino sketch uses the pins in the array order {2, 7, 4, 6, 5, 3}. This only changes the software, not the wiring.
Breadboard bank naming: the image's top half (rows j-f) is mapped to catalogue bank 'b' (rows f-j).

Resistor spans columns 3 and 6 in row h; the orange wire from pin 13 lands in column 3 (row g); LED anode (bent/long leg) in column 6, cathode in column 8; black wire from GND goes to column 8 (row g).
The Arduino GND pin next to AREF/13 is mapped to GND.1.
The sketch code (millis-based blinking) is not part of the physical graph.

Breadboard orientation: in the image the rows f-j are at the top and a-e at the bottom, so the button straddles the centre gap with legs in columns 4 and 6 (4b.f/4t.e and 6b.f/6t.e). The lower rails (next to rows a-e) are mapped to tp (+, red line) and tn (-, black line).
Rail hole numbers (tp.2, tn.2, tp.4, tn.9) are approximated from the image; any hole on the same rail is electrically equivalent.

Pushbutton legs: side 1 (1.l/1.r) is column 4, which goes to 5V via the orange wire; side 2 (2.l/2.r) is column 6, which goes to pin 2 (teal wire) and to the 10k pull-down resistor, whose other end goes to GND via column 9 and a black wire.
The LED on pin 13 is the Uno's built-in LED, so no external LED is added.

The circuit image's lettered rows run j-f above the centre gap and e-a below it; I mapped the upper half to bank 'b' (rows f-j) and the lower half to bank 't' (rows a-e) to match the catalogue naming. The top rail with the red + line is 'tp' and the lower rail is 'bn'. Exact rail hole numbers are approximate; each rail is one strip so connectivity is unaffected.

Each button's top pair of legs (side 1) goes to 5V via a red jumper; its bottom pair (side 2) carries the signal wire to the Leonardo pin and the 10k pulldown resistor to GND. Pin 6 = mouse click, 5 = right, 4 = left, 3 = down, 2 = up, per the sketch.
Resistor values are in ohms (10000 = 10k). The USB cable to the computer is mentioned in the text but is not a circuit part, so it is not in the graph.

Breadboard hole names follow the catalogue: the half with rows f-j (top of the picture) is bank 'b', and the half with rows a-e is bank 't'. Rail hole numbers (bp.1, bp.3, bn.1, bn.7) are approximate. Each rail is one strip, so the exact number does not change the connectivity.

The pushbutton straddles the centre gap at columns 4 and 6. I assumed the pairs joined inside it are the two legs in the same column. So side 1 is column 4 (5V side) and side 2 is column 6 (pin 2 and resistor side). This matches the schematic, where the switch sits between 5V and the pin 2 / pull-down node.

The 10k resistor is on the same side as the input pin (column 6). It runs to column 9, which a black jumper wire connects to the ground rail. The 5V wire (red) feeds the + rail, and an orange wire takes it from the + rail to the button's column 4.
The Uno GND on the power header is taken as GND.2. The manual does not say which GND pin.

The resistor count of 3 is a false positive. The graph has exactly two fixed resistors, r1 (10k) and r2 (220 ohm), matching the parts list. The third counted item is the photoresistor ldr1 (type 'photoresistor'), which is the manual's required analog sensor and appears in the circuit image, the schematic and the text. It is kept deliberately, because removing it would break the circuit.
Breadboard coordinates follow the circuit image's row labels: the upper half of the image is rows f-j, which the catalogue calls bank 'b'. The lower half (rows a-e) is bank 't' and is unused.
Rail hole numbers (tp.2, tn.4, tp.6, tn.13, tn.26) are approximate. They are read from the image, and any hole on the same rail is electrically equivalent.

In the image the LED is wired as pin 9 -> LED anode (col 22), LED cathode (col 23) -> 220 ohm resistor -> GND rail. The schematic puts the resistor before the LED. Both are a series connection, and the image was used as the authority.
The LED leg that bends (longer leg) is taken as the anode and is the one connected to the blue pin 9 wire.
The Uno has several GND pins. The black wire goes to the lower GND pin in the power header, which is GND.2 here.
The manual's circuit text mentions 'Analog input 2' but the image and schematic use A0. A0 is used.
The 10k resistor is the resistor between the photoresistor/A0 node and the GND rail, and forms a voltage divider with the photoresistor from 5V.
The image shows the breadboard with rows f-j in the top half. In the catalogue's naming the f-j half is bank 'b', so the circuit uses bank 'b' holes.
Column positions were read from the image: orange wire in column 3 (row g), resistor from column 3 to column 6 (row h), LED legs in columns 6 and 8 (row i), black wire in column 8 (row h).

The text says the long leg (anode) connects to the resistor output and the short leg (cathode) connects to ground. In the image the bent, longer leg is in column 6 with the resistor, so that leg is A.
The GND header pin next to pin 13 is used for the Arduino end of the black wire, named GND.1.
The USB cable to the computer is not drawn in the circuit, so it is not included. Processing and Max/MSP are software only.
Breadboard coordinates are estimated from the image: the image's upper half (rows f-j) is catalogue bank 'b' and the lower half (rows a-e) is bank 't'.
The bottom power rail: the upper line (black marker) is treated as ground 'bn' and the lower line (red +) as 5V 'bp'. Hole numbers on the rails are approximate; each rail is a single strip.
The pushbutton straddles the centre gap in columns 4 and 6. Column 4 side (side 1) goes to 5V. Column 6 side (side 2) goes to pin 2 and to the 10k pull-down resistor, which runs to the GND rail.
The black wire from the Uno goes to the second GND pin (GND.2) on the power header.
The 10k resistor is written as value=10000 (ohms).
The breadboard image labels its upper half rows f-j; the catalogue names the upper half bank 't' (rows a-e). Holes were mapped by column strip, so only the column matters electrically.

Resistor spans columns 4 and 6, LED anode (bent, longer leg) in column 6, cathode in column 8, as read from the image. Orange wire goes to column 4; black wire goes to column 8 and then to the Uno GND pin next to AREF (GND.1).
Circuit: pin 9 -> 220 ohm resistor -> LED anode; LED cathode -> GND. The 220 ohm value comes from the manual's parts list and schematic.
The breadboard in the image is drawn with rows j-f in the upper half; these map to catalogue bank 'b' (rows f-j), with columns as printed.
LED anode is the bent (longer) leg at column 6; cathode at column 8, connected to GND via the black wire.
The resistor spans columns 3 to 6 on row h; the orange wire from pin 9 enters column 3 (row g), sharing the strip with the resistor's first leg.
Black wire goes to the GND header pin next to pin 13 (GND.1).
The manual's text lists 220 ohm; resistor value set accordingly.
The tutorial allows any analog sensor; the circuit image and schematic show a potentiometer, so that is what was built.

In the image the potentiometer's wiper pin is on the top half of the breadboard in column 12 (yellow wire in the same column strip). Its outer legs are in columns 11 and 13 on the bottom half. I placed the wiper at 12t.f and the yellow wire at 12t.g.
The black wire goes to the GND pin in the Uno power header. I used GND.1 because the image doesn't make clear which of the two GND pins it is.
The potentiometer outer legs are interchangeable (GND=VCC). I took GND from the black wire's column and 5V from the red wire's column, as in the image.
Wire 1 (red) carries 5V, wire 2 (black) carries GND and wire 3 (yellow) carries the wiper signal to A0. The USB cable to the PC is not drawn in the circuit, so I left it out.
The LED on pin 13 is the Uno's built-in LED, so no external LED or resistor is added, as the tutorial's parts list says.

In the image the potentiometer straddles the centre gap. Its two outer legs (GND and 5V) sit in the lower half of the breadboard, in column 10 and column 12. Its wiper leg sits in column 11 of the upper half, and the yellow wire plugs into the same column strip. Using the catalogue's bank naming, the image's lower half (rows a-e) is bank 't' and the upper half (rows f-j) is bank 'b'.
The black wire goes to the second GND pin in the Uno's power header, which I mapped to GND.2.
The potentiometer is shown as a trimmer. I mapped the left leg to GND, the right leg to VCC (5V) and the wiper to SIG. GND and VCC are interchangeable in the catalogue.
All parts exist in the catalogue, so no lookup or new part types were needed.

Each LED sits in two adjacent columns in the top half of the breadboard (anode at columns 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22; cathode in the next column). A 220 ohm resistor bridges the centre gap in the anode column, and a blue jumper runs from the Arduino pin to that column's bottom half.
Arduino pins 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 feed LEDs 1 to 6, left to right, as in the image.
Each LED cathode goes through a short black jumper to the top negative rail, and one black wire joins that rail to the Arduino GND next to pin 13/AREF. I used GND.1 for it.
Breadboard row letters follow the catalogue naming (top half = bank t, bottom half = bank b). The exact row in each strip is arbitrary because all holes in a strip are connected.
The schematic and image show only 220 ohm resistors with no pull-ups or other parts, so none were added.
No external resistor or LED: the tutorial uses the internal pull-up on pin 2 (INPUT_PULLUP) and the Uno's onboard LED on pin 13.

The breadboard image labels the half nearest the top as rows f-j and the lower half as rows a-e. Following the catalogue, the lower half (rows a-e) is bank 't' and the upper half (rows f-j) is bank 'b'. The button straddles the centre gap in columns 10 and 12.

Pushbutton sides are mapped so the two legs in column 10 are one side (1.l, 1.r) and the two legs in column 12 are the other side (2.l, 2.r). This is the only mapping that gives a working switch with the wires in columns 10 and 12 as drawn. Pressing joins column 10 (pin 2) to column 12 (GND).
The black wire goes to the second GND pin on the Uno's power header, which is mapped to GND.2.
The wires are drawn in row c of the lower half (rows a-e). The exact row does not matter because the whole column strip is one node.
No resistor: the sketch uses INPUT_PULLUP, so pin 2 is pulled high internally and the button pulls it to ground.
Button straddles the centre gap in columns 4 and 6. Rows f-j are bank 'b' and rows a-e are bank 't', following the image row labels.
Pin 2 goes by blue wire to column 6 (row i, bank b). GND goes by black wire to column 4 (row c, bank t).
Which button legs form side 1 and side 2 is assumed: column 4 is side 1 and column 6 is side 2, so pressing the button joins pin 2 to GND.
The GND wire goes to the Leonardo's first GND header pin, taken as GND.1.
The Leonardo, breadboard, pushbutton, resistor and jumper wire are all in the catalogue, so no lookup was needed and no new part types were added.
The circuit image shows the button wired to pin 4 on the Leonardo. The schematic labels it pin 2. The text and the image both say pin 4, so I used pin 4.
The button straddles the centre gap in columns 6 and 8. I treated column 6 (1.l top, 1.r bottom) as side 1 and column 8 as side 2, so pressing the button joins column 6 to column 8.
In the image the bottom half of the breadboard is labelled rows a-e. The catalogue calls that bank 't', so I used 't' for it and 'b' for the top half (rows f-j).
The lower rail pair is mapped as bn (upper row, black, ground) and bp (lower row, red, +5V). The exact rail hole numbers are approximate readings from the image.
The USB cable to the computer is not drawn in the circuit or listed in the parts, so it is not included.
The 10k resistor goes from the pin 4 strip (column 6) to the ground rail as a pull-down. The other button side (column 8) goes to 5V through a short red jumper to the + rail.
